reasoning_trace.value: The paper proposes an architecture for an optical transport network that supports integrated sensing and communication services. The system uses a distributed passive wireless radar principle, where 6G Base Stations generate communication signals that are reflected on objects in the surrounding area, creating IQ echo streams. These streams are transmitted to a multi-access edge computing node for storage and processing. A sensing app analyzes the quality of the IQ echo streams and decides which ones can be used for sensing. The app's output is passed to a network orchestrator that determines the optimal transport network configuration to support both communication and sensing services.

The system architecture exploits an optoelectronic transport network interconnecting the Radio Access Network with the core functions located at the MEC. The proposed architecture supports joint sensing and communication services using 3GPP compliant RF signals. The sensing app implements a passive OFDM-based radar that uses reflected signals to estimate object positions. The network orchestrator calculates the optimal resource allocation policy to accommodate both communication and sensing services.

The paper presents numerical results for the proposed scheme, evaluating three different management policies: a) 'single' echo approach, b) 'optimal' dynamic approach, and c) 'all-active' approach. The results show that the 'optimal' approach has higher network requirements compared to the 'single' echo approach (~15%) and is 30% more efficient than the static 'all-active' approach. The 'optimal' scheme receives echoes of similar SNR with the 'all-active' approach, while requiring 50% less network resources.

The proposed architecture has the potential to optimize the operation of an optical transport network supporting ISAC services. The use of an all-optical switch allows for transparent transport of sensing flows, eliminating transmission delays introduced by optoelectronic devices. The 'optimal' approach has higher network requirements compared to the 'single' echo approach but is more efficient than the 'all-active' approach. The results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed architecture in supporting joint sensing and communication services.
